drapeaux.note: The tagline says that in 1949 two rival record companies each launch a new format, but the body dates Columbia's LP to June 21, 1948 and only RCA's 45 to 1949.

titre: The Speed War Between the 33 rpm and the 45 rpm
accroche: In 1949, two rival record companies each launch a new disc format: at a different speed, and incompatible with the other's.
contenu_vulgarise:
On June 21, 1948, at the Waldorf Astoria in New York, Columbia Records gathers the press to present an invention by its chief engineer Peter Goldmark: a twelve-inch (thirty-centimeter) disc, cut with a microscopic groove, that turns at 33 and a third revolutions per minute and holds twenty-three minutes per side. Until then, the standard disc, the 78 rpm, lasts no more than four to five minutes per side before it has to be flipped. Columbia has just invented the long-playing album.

## RCA's riposte locks in the player, not just the disc

RCA Victor, Columbia's great rival, refuses to pay a license to adopt this new format. In 1949, the company answers with its own disc: seven inches in diameter, turning at 45 revolutions per minute. Technically, these two inventions are not head-on opposites: Columbia's 33 aims at the album, RCA's 45 aims at the single track, with a large center hole designed for its own automatic changer, which stacks several discs and chains the songs together without intervention. But in practice, each of the two companies imposes its own equipment: a record player bought to play Columbia does not play RCA, and vice versa. For nearly two years, a listener who follows both catalogs has to own two machines.

## What it shifts

The story usually remembered from such a clash of formats is that of a single winner, as VHS beat Betamax. Here, that is not what happened. RCA Victor announces in January 1950 its intention to produce 33s of its own: on that ground, Columbia has won. But RCA's 45, far from disappearing, becomes the market standard for the single track for the following decades, popularized by the jukeboxes of bars and fairgrounds that draw from it precisely their compact format and wide hole. In 1952, four years after the launch of the 33, it still accounts for only 26% of record sales by value in the United States, against 25% for the 45: the two share the market rather than one camp eliminating the other. What the industry ended up acknowledging was not the victory of one format over the other, but a division of roles: the album on 33, the single on 45, a split that structured the sale of recorded music until the arrival of the CD.

repere.texte: In 1952, four years after its launch, the 33 rpm still accounts for only 26% of record sales by value in the United States, against 25% for RCA's 45: neither format eliminated the other.

carte.punch: 1948: Columbia invents the album. 1949: RCA answers with an incompatible disc.
carte.idee: Columbia launches the 33 in 1948, RCA the 45 in 1949: two incompatible formats, two machines to own. RCA gives in in 1950 and starts pressing 33s too. But the 45 does not disappear: it becomes the format of the single for decades.

quiz.question: How did the speed war between Columbia's 33 rpm and RCA's 45 rpm actually end?
choix: RCA eventually bought Columbia Records to end the conflict
The 45 quickly disappeared, unable to compete with Columbia's 33
The two formats coexisted, each dominating a different segment: the album for one, the single for the other
The federal government imposed a single format on both companies
quiz.explication: RCA ended up producing 33s itself in 1950, but its own format, the 45, did not disappear for that: it became the standard for the single for decades. No buyout or government intervention ended the conflict: it was a division of the market, not the elimination of one camp.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who presents Columbia's new disc on June 21, 1948, at the Waldorf Astoria?
choix: Thomas Edison, inventor of the phonograph
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Peter Goldmark, chief engineer of Columbia Records, who presents the press with the new 33 and a third rpm disc, on June 21, 1948, at the Waldorf Astoria in New York.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does RCA Victor launch its own disc format in 1949 rather than adopt Columbia's?
choix: Columbia formally forbids it from using its patent
Its pressing equipment is incompatible with the 33 rpm format
It refuses to pay a license to use Columbia's invention
It wants to compete directly with the 78 rpm market
quiz_supplementaire.explication: RCA Victor refuses to pay a license to adopt Columbia's invention and answers in 1949 with its own, incompatible format rather than aligning with the 33.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does RCA Victor do in January 1950, marking its defeat on the album front?
choix: It sues Columbia for unfair competition
It permanently withdraws the 45 from the market
It announces its intention to produce 33s of its own as well
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In January 1950, RCA Victor announces that it will itself produce 33s, acknowledging its defeat on the album front against Columbia's invention.
